# Requirement #2283: Generator and analyzer crash with IndexOutOfRangeException on a closed generic struct from a referenced assembly

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2283

#### Bug description

Both `MessagePackGenerator` (CS8785) and `MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer` (AD0001) throw `IndexOutOfRangeException` when a `[MessagePackObject]` type has a member whose type is a **closed generic value type defined in a referenced assembly**.

Because the generator then "will not contribute to the output", the compiling assembly silently ends up with **no generated resolver at all**. It is only a warning, so a normal build looks fine, but trimmed and NativeAOT apps fail at runtime. In our case three assemblies of a large app had been shipping without a resolver across two releases before we noticed.

#### Repro steps

Two projects. `lib`:

```csharp
using MessagePack;
namespace Lib;

[MessagePackObject]
public partial record struct Item<T>([property: Key(0)] string Key);
```

`app`, with a `ProjectReference` to `lib`:

```csharp
using MessagePack; using Lib;
namespace App;

[MessagePackObject]
public sealed partial record Cmd([property: Key(0)] string Scope)
{
    [Key(1)] public Item<int> Member { get; init; }
}
```

Then `dotnet build` on `app`. Both projects are in the attached `mp-repro.zip`.

#### Expected behavior

A clean build, with a generated resolver in `app`.

#### Actual behavior

```
CSC : warning CS8785: Generator 'MessagePackGenerator' failed to generate source. It will not
contribute to the output and compilation errors may occur as a result. Exception was of type
'IndexOutOfRangeException' with message 'Index was outside the bounds of the array.'.
CSC : warning AD0001: Analyzer 'MessagePack.SourceGenerator.Analyzers.MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer'
threw an exception of type 'System.IndexOutOfRangeException' with message 'Index was outside the
bounds of the array.'.
```

`app.dll` contains no `GeneratedMessagePackResolver`.

- Version used: MessagePack 3.1.8
- Runtime: .NET 10 (SDK 10.0.204), Windows 11

#### Additional context

**What triggers it.** `Item` is declared in `lib`, `Cmd` in `app`:

| `Item` declared as | result |
|---|---|
| `record struct Item<T>` | **crash** |
| `struct Item<T>` | **crash** |
| `struct Item` | ok |
| `record struct Item` | ok |
| `class Item<T>` | ok |
| `record class Item<T>` | ok |

So it needs all three of: **generic**, **value type**, **from a referenced assembly**. Moving the identical `Item<T>` declaration into `app` itself makes the crash disappear, which is what makes this specific to metadata symbols.

**Stack trace.**

```
System.IndexOutOfRangeException: Index was outside the bounds of the array.
   at TypeCollector.GetObjectInfo(INamedTypeSymbol formattedType, ISymbol callerSymbol)
   at TypeCollector.CollectGeneric(INamedTypeSymbol type, ISymbol callerSymbol) in TypeCollector.cs:line 661
   at TypeCollector.CollectCore(ITypeSymbol typeSymbol, ISymbol callerSymbol) in TypeCollector.cs:line 371
   at TypeCollector.GetObjectInfo(INamedTypeSymbol formattedType, ISymbol callerSymbol) in TypeCollector.cs:line 1062
   at TypeCollector.CollectCore(ITypeSymbol typeSymbol, ISymbol callerSymbol) in TypeCollector.cs:line 386
   at TypeCollector.Collect() in TypeCollector.cs:line 300
   at MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer.AnalyzeSymbol(SymbolAnalysisContext, ReferenceSymbols, AnalyzerOptions) in MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer.cs:line 431
```

`CollectGeneric` line 661 is the closed-generic branch that calls `GetObjectInfo` directly:

```csharp
else
{
    // NOTE: ... closed generic types such as `Foo<string>` are not registered as a formatter.
    this.GetObjectInfo(type, callerSymbol);
```

so `GetObjectInfo` runs against a type that has no syntax. Several diagnostic paths inside it index `DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0]` directly (lines 735, 1009, 1101) instead of using `FirstOrDefault()` the way the neighbouring `GetIdentifierLocation` / `GetLocation` / `GetParameterListLocation` helpers already do, and that collection is empty for a metadata symbol. I did not narrow down which of the three fires.

**Workaround.** Putting `[MessagePackFormatter(typeof(ItemFormatter<>))]` on the generic value type short-circuits `CollectCore` (line 356) before `GetObjectInfo` is reached, at the cost of hand-writing the formatter.

**Possibly related:** #2092 reports CS8785 from the v3 generator, but with a different inner exception and no repro.

requirement_points.text: When a [MessagePackObject] type has a member whose type is a closed generic value type (struct or record struct) declared in a referenced assembly, the source generator completes without throwing IndexOutOfRangeException (no CS8785).
Under the same conditions, the MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer completes without throwing IndexOutOfRangeException (no AD0001).
The consuming assembly still receives a generated MessagePack resolver (such as GeneratedMessagePackResolver) instead of silently producing none.
Diagnostics about members of a type defined in a referenced assembly are not reported in the consuming compilation; they are left to the assembly that defines the type.
The fix covers both plain generic structs and generic record structs coming from metadata.

plants.description: GetPropertyIdentifierLocation indexes DeclaringSyntaxReferences with [0] instead of FirstOrDefault(). For a property that comes from metadata (a referenced assembly) the collection is empty, so this throws IndexOutOfRangeException again and the generator/analyzer fail with CS8785/AD0001.

The MemberNeedsKey diagnostic uses First() instead of FirstOrDefault() when locating the member. Members of types that come from metadata have no DeclaringSyntaxReferences, so First() throws and the analyzer crashes with AD0001.

The null check on reportAnalyzerDiagnostic is dropped, so in the source generator (where no diagnostic reporter is supplied) reportDiagnostic becomes a non-null delegate wrapping a null callback. Any diagnostic raised then dereferences the null callback and the generator fails with CS8785, leaving the assembly with no generated resolver.

The location filter now also accepts Location.None, which is exactly the location that diagnostics about metadata members get. Diagnostics about members of a type defined in a referenced assembly are therefore reported in the consuming compilation, which is what the requirement says must not happen.

The diagnostic reporter is wired up without the ReportIfLocatedInCompilation wrapper, so the metadata-location filtering is gone entirely and diagnostics about members declared in a referenced assembly are reported in the consuming compilation.

The guard inside ReportIfLocatedInCompilation is removed and every diagnostic is forwarded, so diagnostics whose location is not in the compilation being analyzed (i.e. about types and members from referenced assemblies) are reported in the consuming compilation again.

The metadata-safe lookup for the property location is replaced with First(), which throws when the property has no declaration in source. The crash that the change was meant to remove comes back for members of types declared in a referenced assembly.
The MemberNeedsKey diagnostic indexes DeclaringSyntaxReferences directly instead of using the safe lookup, so the analyzer throws again for members that come from metadata rather than source.
The conditional is written with the positive test and the branches swapped; behaviour is identical.
Location.IsInSource is exactly equivalent to Location.SourceTree being non-null, so the guard reads the same way but behaves identically.
Parameter renamed; the body uses the new name and no behaviour changes.
Only parentheses are added around the null-conditional expression; the null propagation is unchanged.

points.reason: The two `DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0]` accesses that threw IndexOutOfRangeException for metadata symbols are replaced with `FirstOrDefault()`-based helpers (`GetPropertyIdentifierLocation` and inline `FirstOrDefault()?.GetSyntax().GetLocation()`), so the generator no longer crashes on closed generic value types from referenced assemblies.
The analyzer shares `TypeCollector` with the generator; the same `FirstOrDefault()` guards prevent the analyzer from throwing AD0001 on metadata-only types.
The new `RunWithMetadataReferenceAsync` helper runs the generator and asserts that the expected resolver hint name (e.g. `App.AppResolver.g.cs`) is present in the generated sources.

`reportDiagnostic` is wrapped by `ReportIfLocatedInCompilation`, which only forwards diagnostics whose location is in a syntax tree contained by the current compilation, so members of referenced-assembly types are never reported in the consuming project.

Separate tests cover a plain generic struct (`ClosedGenericStruct_FromMetadataReference`) and a generic record struct (`ClosedGenericRecordStruct_FromMetadataReference`, the exact issue repro), both declared in a referenced assembly.

findings.message: GetPropertyIdentifierLocation indexes DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0] directly without checking for an empty collection. For a property symbol from metadata (no source declaration), this throws IndexOutOfRangeException, causing the same crash the fix is intended to prevent. It should use FirstOrDefault() like the neighbouring helper methods.

The replacement of the unsafe DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0] access with GetPropertyIdentifierLocation(item) does not make the call safe, because GetPropertyIdentifierLocation itself still indexes DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0] directly.

findings.message: ReportIfLocatedInCompilation is a no-op: it unconditionally forwards every diagnostic to the original callback without checking whether the diagnostic's location belongs to the current compilation. Diagnostics about members of types defined in referenced assemblies (metadata symbols) are therefore still reported in the consuming compilation, violating R4. The method should suppress diagnostics whose Location is not in a source tree of the compilation being analyzed.

# Requirement #2283: Generator and analyzer must report MsgPack004 for an unkeyed member of a closed generic struct from a referenced assembly

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2283

#### Bug description

Both `MessagePackGenerator` and `MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer` silently ignore an unkeyed public member on a **closed generic value type defined in a referenced assembly** when that type is used as a member of a `[MessagePackObject]` type. The consuming project builds cleanly and generates a resolver, but the unkeyed member is omitted from serialization. This is only a runtime failure, so trimmed and NativeAOT apps can ship broken for releases before anyone notices. The analyzer should report `MsgPack004` in the consuming project at the usage of the closed generic type, even though the member itself is declared in metadata.

#### Repro steps

Two projects. `lib`:

```csharp
using MessagePack;
namespace Lib;

[MessagePackObject]
public partial record struct Item<T>([property: Key(0)] string Key)
{
    public int Unkeyed { get; init; }
}
```

`app`, with a `ProjectReference` to `lib`:

```csharp
using MessagePack; using Lib;
namespace App;

[MessagePackObject]
public sealed partial record Cmd([property: Key(0)] string Scope)
{
    [Key(1)] public Item<int> Member { get; init; }
}
```

Then `dotnet build` on `app`. Both projects are in the attached `mp-repro.zip`.

#### Expected behavior

A build with a generated resolver in `app` and a `MsgPack004` diagnostic in `app` pointing at the `Item<int>` member, so the missing key on `Item<int>.Unkeyed` is caught in the consuming project.

#### Actual behavior

The build succeeds with no diagnostic. `app.dll` contains `GeneratedMessagePackResolver`, but `Item<int>.Unkeyed` is not serialized. The analyzer does not report `MsgPack004` because the member is declared in metadata and the diagnostic is dropped.

- Version used: MessagePack 3.1.8
- Runtime: .NET 10 (SDK 10.0.204), Windows 11

#### Additional context

**What triggers it.** `Item` is declared in `lib`, `Cmd` in `app`:

| `Item` declared as | result |
|---|---|
| `record struct Item<T>` with unkeyed member | **no diagnostic** |
| `struct Item<T>` with unkeyed member | **no diagnostic** |
| `struct Item` with unkeyed member | `MsgPack004` |
| `record struct Item` with unkeyed member | `MsgPack004` |
| `class Item<T>` with unkeyed member | `MsgPack004` |
| `record class Item<T>` with unkeyed member | `MsgPack004` |

So it needs all three of: **generic**, **value type**, **from a referenced assembly**. Moving the identical `Item<T>` declaration into `app` itself makes the diagnostic appear, which is what makes this specific to metadata symbols.

**Stack trace.**

```
None. The analyzer returns without reporting a diagnostic.
```

**Workaround.** Putting `[MessagePackFormatter(typeof(ItemFormatter<>))]` on the generic value type avoids the need for a key, at the cost of hand-writing the formatter. Adding `[Key(1)]` to `Unkeyed` in `lib` also works when `lib` is under your control.

**Possibly related:** #2092 reports CS8785 from the v3 generator, but with a different inner exception and no repro.

findings.message: The reportDiagnostic callback is wrapped so that every diagnostic is passed through ReportIfLocatedInCompilation, which drops diagnostics whose location is not in the current compilation's source trees. This means MsgPack004 for an unkeyed member of a closed generic type from a referenced assembly is never reported in the consuming project, which is exactly what the requirement demands.

ReportIfLocatedInCompilation explicitly suppresses diagnostics for metadata-declared members, stating they belong to the defining assembly. This is the opposite of the required behavior, which is for the analyzer to report MsgPack004 in the consuming project at the usage site. No code path reports the diagnostic at the usage location.
